title: Dream Machine: Scaling to 1m users in 4 days — Keegan McCallum, Luma AI

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is serving a trained video model in production: rebuilding the inference stack from Triton to vanilla PyTorch, SLO-based scheduling, burst scaling, and fleet-wide model version management. Dream Machine is a creative video-generation product (media_creative), while the infrastructure and scaling lessons are broadly applicable across AI systems (general_purpose). Content covers initial deployment, production serving, demand-driven scaling, and ongoing operations including scheduling and model rollouts. Requires familiarity with GPU inference serving, distributed systems, and PyTorch deployment as stated in the talk's prerequisites. Conference talk presented at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with grade 'said_in_transcript' and specific evidence anchors.

summary: Keegan McCallum describes Luma AI's launch of Dream Machine on June 11, 2024. The team expected significant traffic but was overwhelmed, exhausting 500 H100 GPUs within the first hour. Their contingency plan involved manually SSH-ing into every available GPU across providers, reaching 5,000 H100s in six hours. Queues of nearly 100,000 requests began draining by 2 p.m., but CEO Amit's tweet announcing 10x scaling reignited demand, prompting the team to take over their 4,000-GPU training cluster. The product hit 1 million users in four days, faster than ChatGPT's five days, processing ~500,000 videos in twelve hours. McCallum frames Luma as a foundation model lab building general multimodal intelligence, not just a video model company, and demonstrates the modify-video feature and public API. On infrastructure, the original Triton-based stack was brittle and poorly suited to multi-GPU/multi-node inference, so the team rebuilt on vanilla PyTorch with decoupled CPU and GPU workers connected via Tailscale to Redis and SeaweedFS, enabling elastic scaling. Back pressure was solved with dispatch limitations, and an SLO-based scheduling system ranks jobs by percentage of worst-case wait time consumed, preventing work starvation across user tiers. A Slurm-based scheduler handles bursts by scaling onto the training cluster. For model management, Luma adopted Triton's model repository concept: every model has a folder in object storage with immutable versioned subfolders containing the full Python environment and checkpoints, with a YAML file defining the active version. This enables reproducible rollbacks and automated on-the-fly version switching across thousands of GPUs without restarting workers. In Q&A, McCallum explained that a dedicated ~10-person 'Excel team' optimizes low-level PyTorch operations for new chipsets, working closely with Nvidia and AMD, and exploring others through partnerships including Humane/Groq. He noted the application uses VLMs to caption uploaded video/image inputs to enhance prompts, with true VQA potentially coming. He closed with a hiring call for engineers, researchers, and AI enthusiasts.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Launch Day and Initial Scaling
sections.summary: McCallum describes Dream Machine's launch on June 11, 2024. 500 H100 GPUs were quickly exhausted. A manual SSH-based contingency plan scaled to 5,000 GPUs in six hours. Queues of ~100,000 drained by 2 p.m., but CEO Amit's tweet about 10x scaling reignited demand. The team then took over their 4,000-GPU training cluster. The product reached 1 million users in four days and processed ~500,000 videos in twelve hours.

sections.title: Luma AI Mission and Product Demo
sections.summary: Luma is a foundation model lab building general multimodal intelligence, not just a video model company. McCallum demonstrates a 'modify video' feature where iPhone videos are transformed via text prompts. He highlights the public API and SDK for developers, noting Luma handles prompt engineering internally.

sections.title: Serving Stack Re-architecture
sections.summary: The original tightly-coupled container stack with Triton inference server was brittle, unsuitable for multi-GPU/multi-node inference, lacked chipset flexibility, and was hard for researchers. The team rebuilt on vanilla PyTorch with decoupled CPU workers (pre-loading multimedia) and GPU workers connectable via Tailscale to Redis and SeaweedFS, enabling elastic scaling across providers and the training cluster.

sections.title: Scaling Challenges: Back Pressure, Fair Scheduling, Bursts
sections.summary: Back pressure was solved with dispatch limitations capping queued jobs per cluster. Fair scheduling across user tiers used an SLO-based system implemented by Saurish: jobs ranked by percentage of worst-case wait time consumed, providing intuitive fair scheduling and preventing work starvation. A Slurm-based scheduler automatically scales inference onto the training cluster during bursts, which researchers dislike. Queue management is the team's least favorite task.

sections.title: Model Management and Versioning
sections.summary: Luma adopted Triton's model repository concept: every model has a folder in object storage with immutable versioned subfolders containing the full Python environment and checkpoints. A YAML file defines the active version. This enables reproducible rollbacks and running models in disparate environments consistently. An automated rollout system updates workers on-the-fly when YAML files change, allowing fleet-wide version switching across thousands of H100 and AMD GPUs without restarts, replacing the early days of parallel SSH.

sections.title: Hiring, Q&A, and Chipset Partnerships
sections.summary: McCallum announces Luma is actively hiring engineers, researchers, and AI enthusiasts. In Q&A, he explains that chip providers ensure PyTorch compatibility for their chipsets, while a dedicated ~10-person 'Excel team' optimizes low-level PyTorch operations using tools like Triton. Luma works closely with Nvidia and AMD and is exploring other chipsets through partnerships including Humane (working with Groq). Cloud providers deliver Kubernetes clusters but Luma does not provision nodes directly. The application uses VLMs to caption uploaded video/image inputs to enhance prompts, with true VQA potentially coming.
